title: Key Inequality: log(1+t) > t/(1+t)
content: For t > 0, t/(1+t) < log(1+t). Proof: apply Real.add_one_lt_exp to x = -t/(1+t) ≠ 0. Get 1/(1+t) < exp(-t/(1+t)). Take log of both sides (1/(1+t) > 0), then use log_inv to rewrite log(1/(1+t)) = -log(1+t).
mathContext: Real.add_one_lt_exp: x ≠ 0 → 1+x < exp(x). Applied to -t/(1+t) and then log taken of both sides.

title: Derivative of g(t) = log(1+t)/t is Negative
content: HasDerivAt (log(1+·)/·) ((t/(1+t) - log(1+t))/t²) t, and this derivative is strictly negative. The HasDerivAt is computed via the quotient rule (HasDerivAt.div). The negativity uses the key inequality: t/(1+t) < log(1+t) implies the numerator is negative.
mathContext: g'(t) = (1/(1+t)·t - log(1+t))/t². The numerator equals t/(1+t) - log(1+t) < 0 by log_one_plus_gt.

title: g(t) = log(1+t)/t is Strictly Decreasing on (0,∞)
content: StrictAntiOn (log(1+·)/·) (Ioi 0). The proof applies strictAntiOn_of_deriv_neg (convex_Ioi 0), providing continuity (ContinuousOn) and the negative derivative (via HasDerivAt.deriv to convert HasDerivAt to deriv).
mathContext: strictAntiOn_of_deriv_neg: on a convex set, continuous f with negative deriv everywhere is strictly anti-monotone.

title: Main: (1+1/m)^m < (1+1/n)^n for 1 ≤ m < n
content: one_plus_inv_pow_strictMono: for 1 ≤ m < n, (1+1/m)^m < (1+1/n)^n. Proof: rewrite both sides as exp(log(...)), use exp_lt_exp + log_pow + push_cast, then apply nlog_strictMono which compares g(1/m) < g(1/n) via the strict anti-monotonicity of g and 1/n < 1/m.
mathContext: (1+1/n)^n = exp(n·log(1+1/n)) = exp(g(1/n)). StrictAntiOn g + 1/n < 1/m ⟹ g(1/n) > g(1/m) ⟹ exp comparison.

title: Bounds: 2 < (1+1/n)^n < 3
content: Lower bound: (1+1/1)^1 = 2, so strict monotonicity gives 2 < (1+1/n)^n for n ≥ 2. Upper bound: 1+1/n ≤ exp(1/n) by Real.add_one_le_exp, so (1+1/n)^n ≤ exp(1/n)^n = exp(n·(1/n)) = exp(1). Since exp(1) < 3 by Real.exp_one_lt_d9, the bound follows.
mathContext: The upper bound uses (1+x)^n ≤ exp(x·n) via the Bernoulli-type inequality, then Real.exp_nat_mul to simplify exp(1/n)^n = exp(1).
